text: Cryogenic Hydrogen Production: Losses and Mitigation Strategies As noted in Figure 42, the primary cause of hydrogen losses in the liquefaction step is leakage through equipment. Cooper et al. (2022) estimate hydrogen losses from liquefaction of 0.15%– 2.21%. An important quantum mechanics phenomenon that occurs during the hydrogen liquefaction process is the conversion of ortho-hydrogen (hydrogen with protons that spin in same direction) into para-hydrogen (hydrogen with protons that spin in opposite directions) as temperature decreases (Al Ghafri et al. 2022). This phenomenon directly correlates to downstream boil-off losses because the conversion process is exothermic. If the liquefaction process does not effectively convert ortho-hydrogen to para-hydrogen, the conversion process will occur while the LH is in storage, releasing heat and causing hydrogen vaporization. To 2 mitigate any hydrogen losses due to ortho-to-para hydrogen conversion, plant operators must be aware of the proper hydrogen residence times within the system for the full conversion process to occur and should not cut corners to deliver product at a faster rate. 4.2.1.2 Cryogenic Hydrogen Transportation: Losses and Mitigation Strategies In Section 4.1.2 we mention that the primary method of transporting LH today is via tanker 2 trucks, with ocean tankers and railcars as alternative transport methods that are under development. The transportation step is necessary in the case where liquid hydrogen is not directly produced at the airport. If liquid hydrogen transport to the airport is required, there are several possible points in the delivery process where hydrogen losses can occur. These include losses during tank transfers at the origin and destination and losses en route. During tank transfers, liquid hydrogen is typically lost to the environment via intentional purges to the transfer lines, leakage through equipment, and LH boil-off that is eventually vented. Liquid 2 67 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. hydrogen losses during the transfer step are reported as high as 10%–20% per transfer (Esquivel- Elizondo et al. 2023; GenH2 2024; Clean Energy Group 2025). As liquid hydrogen is transferred between tanks, there are several strategies and technologies that operators make use of to minimize boil-off. Standard practice is to use vacuum-insulated transfer lines that are precooled before transfers. Transfers are typically done using pressure-based or pumped-based methods. To minimize boil-off further, operators should consider high efficiency liquid hydrogen pumps over pressure-based tank transfers (Gil-Esmendia et al. 2025). Variable speed drive pumps have shown to be effective at transferring LH with low energy dissipation 2 (Krog and Berstad 2025). Manufacturers of liquid hydrogen pumps include Bosch Rexroth, Cryostar, Barber Nichols, and others (Bosch Rexroth, n.d.; Cryostar, n.d.; Barber Nichols, n.d.). Other strategies include using slow fill rates to reduce energy losses as heat, using refrigerated transfer lines (GenH2 n.d.-a), and/or transferring liquid hydrogen in a subcooled state such that the hydrogen can take in additional heat without vaporizing (Daimler Truck 2024).
